chapter.name: The Colonial Era in India
chapter.blurb: Under Theme B, Tapestry of the Past. What colonialism was, the Portuguese, Dutch and French in India, the East India Company's rise from trader to ruler, famines and the drain of wealth, colonial industry, governance and education, early resistance, the Great Rebellion of 1857 and the legacy of colonial rule.

concepts.name: What Colonialism Was and the Age of Colonialism
concepts.description: The meaning of colonialism, its long history before Europe, the European expansion from the 15th century, the four motives behind it, and the gap between the claimed 'civilising mission' and what colonised peoples actually experienced.
concepts.idea: Colonialism is one country taking control of another region and imposing its own political, economic and cultural systems on it.
concepts.rule: Colonialism is not recent: it can be traced to the great empires of the 1st millennium BCE, and in the 1st millennium CE the spread of Christianity and Islam also involved colonising the territories converted to the new faiths. The phrase 'Age of Colonialism' usually means Europe's expansion from the 15th century onward, led by Spain, Portugal, Britain, France and the Netherlands, across Africa, Asia, the Americas, Australia and many Pacific islands. Four motives drove it: political competition between European powers, economic advantage (new resources, markets, trade routes and plunder), conversion of indigenous populations to Christianity, and, to a lesser degree, scientific inquiry. Colonisers claimed a 'civilising mission', but the reality was loss of independence, exploitation of resources, destruction of traditional ways of life and the imposition of foreign cultural values. Colonialism declined in the mid-20th century, especially after World War II.
concepts.example: A coloniser would call the people it ruled 'savage' or 'primitive' while taking their resources. That gap between the claimed mission and the real result is what the chapter asks you to notice.

questions.q: Colonialism existed long before the 15th century, yet the chapter reserves the phrase 'Age of Colonialism' for Europe's expansion. Analyse why, using two features of that expansion.
questions.a: The chapter itself says colonialism is old, going back to the empires of the 1st millennium BCE and the religious expansions of the 1st millennium CE, so the phrase is not about being first. It is reserved for Europe's expansion because of its scale and its method. In scale, within a few centuries it extended to large parts of the world at once -- Africa, Asia, the Americas, Australia and many Pacific islands. In method, the conquests were often achieved through military campaigns involving the massacre or enslavement of native populations, and were justified by a claimed 'civilising mission' that turned temporary conquest into long-term political, economic and cultural control.
s: Acknowledges that colonialism is older than the 15th century

concepts.name: India's Wealth and the Portuguese in India
concepts.description: India's economic standing before European colonisation, and the Portuguese presence from Vasco da Gama's arrival in 1498 through Goa, the cartaz permit system, the spice monopoly, the Goa Inquisition and the resistance at Ullal.
concepts.idea: India was one of the world's two largest economies, and that wealth is exactly what drew the first European colonial power to her shores.
concepts.rule: India traded with the Greeks and Romans over two millennia ago; spices, cotton, ivory, gems, sandalwood, teakwood and wootz steel were sought after in the Mediterranean world. Until the 16th century CE India contributed at least one-fourth of world GDP (an estimate by the economist Angus Maddison), making her one of the two largest economies alongside China. That prosperity made her an attractive target. Vasco da Gama reached Kappad near Kozhikode in May 1498 and was well received, but on his second voyage four years later he seized, tortured and killed Indian merchants and bombarded Calicut from the sea. The Portuguese took strategic ports including Goa in 1510, which became their colonial capital, and imposed the cartaz, a pass every ship in the Arabian Sea had to buy; ships without one were seized, which gave them a near-century monopoly of the spice trade. At Goa they set up the Inquisition in 1560 (abolished only in 1812), persecuting Hindus, Muslims, Jews and converts suspected of practising their original faith, with forced conversions and the destruction of many Hindu temples.
concepts.example: At Ullal in present-day southern Karnataka, Rani Abbakka I formed alliances with neighbouring kingdoms and thwarted repeated Portuguese attempts on the port; Rani Abbakka II is said to have made fireballs from coconut shells and burnt several Portuguese ships. Both are remembered in Yakshagana dance-drama.

concepts.name: The Dutch and the French in India
concepts.description: The Dutch commercial presence and their defeat at Colachel in 1741, and the French at Pondicherry under Dupleix, who invented the sepoy army and indirect rule before losing the Carnatic Wars to the British.
concepts.idea: Neither the Dutch nor the French built a lasting empire in India, but the French left behind the methods the British would later use to build theirs.
concepts.rule: The Dutch arrived in the early 17th century and, unlike the Portuguese, focused primarily on commercial dominance, particularly the spice trade. Their Dutch East India Company held posts at Surat, Bharuch and Cochin on the west coast and Nagapattinam and Masulipatnam on the east, and was strongest in Malabar, where it displaced the Portuguese from several trading centres. Their presence declined sharply after the Battle of Colachel in 1741, where Travancore under King Marthanda Varma defeated them on land and at sea -- a rare instance of an Asian power repelling a European colonial force. The French set up at Surat in 1668 and Pondicherry in 1674, where their Compagnie des Indes Orientales planned a French empire in India. Dupleix, Governor-General of French India from 1742 to 1754, pioneered two strategies the British later adopted: training Indian soldiers in European military techniques to create disciplined infantry called sepoys, and indirect rule through puppet Indian rulers installed by intervening in succession disputes. French ambitions were checked in the Carnatic Wars of 1746 to 1763; despite Dupleix's capture of Madras in 1746 the colony was reduced to Pondicherry and a few smaller enclaves.
concepts.example: Like the Dutch, and unlike the Portuguese, the French did not much intervene in Indians' social and religious life. The rare exception was the destruction in 1748 of Pondicherry's large Vedapurishwaran temple, ordered by Dupleix on the persistent request of the town's Jesuit priests and of his own wife.

concepts.name: From Traders to Rulers: the East India Company and 'Divide and Rule'
concepts.description: How a trading company became an imperial power: the royal charter, the coastal footholds, the 'divide and rule' strategy, the Battle of Plassey, the Doctrine of Lapse, princely states and the subsidiary alliance system.
concepts.idea: The British takeover of India was gradual, calculated and disguised as commerce, not a single conquest.
concepts.rule: The English East India Company began as a trading company with a royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I that gave it special powers, including the right to raise a private army. Its agents kept up a pretence of being mere traders, which let them establish coastal footholds at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta with minimal resistance, since local rulers generally welcomed foreign trade. They then cultivated political relationships, offering military support to some rulers against their rivals, playing on succession disputes and encouraging tensions between religious communities -- the 'divide and rule' policy. At Plassey in 1757 Robert Clive conspired with Mir Jafar, Siraj-ud-daulah's military commander, promising him the throne; Mir Jafar's forces stood aside and the smaller British force won. As kingmakers the Company then expanded directly, through the Doctrine of Lapse, which annexed any princely state whose ruler died without a natural male heir and so disregarded the Hindu tradition of adoption, and indirectly, through subsidiary alliances, under which a British Resident sat in the ruler's court while the ruler paid for British troops and conducted foreign relations only through the British.
concepts.example: Hyderabad's ruler was among the first to enter a subsidiary alliance, in 1798. The system let Britain control vast territories without the administrative costs of direct rule -- what was called 'an empire on the cheap'.

concepts.name: Devastating Famines under Colonial Rule
concepts.description: How colonial revenue policy, continued grain exports, 'free market' doctrine and inadequate relief turned crop failures into the famines of 1770-1772 and 1876-1878, and what the total cost was.
concepts.idea: Famines had always occurred in India, but never on the colonial scale, because policy now made a bad harvest into a catastrophe.
concepts.rule: A few years after Plassey the East India Company secured the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, some of India's richest regions, and its agents extracted maximum revenue while investing minimally in governance or development. In 1770-1772, on top of two years of crop failure, harsh revenue targets requiring a high rate of cash taxes regardless of harvest conditions caused a famine that killed nearly one-third of Bengal's population, an estimated 10 million people; the Company even increased the land tax during it. During the Great Famine of 1876-1878 up to 8 million perished, mostly in the Deccan plateau, while the administration continued exporting grain -- about one million tonnes of rice a year -- and the 'free market' policy left food prices free to rise. Lord Lytton, the Viceroy, ordered that there was to be no interference of any kind by the Government aimed at reducing the price of food, and in 1876, at the famine's height, staged a durbar in Delhi with a week-long feast for 68,000 guests. Estimates of severe famines under British rule run from a dozen to over 20, with total victims put at between 50 and 100 million.

concepts.name: The Drain of India's Wealth
concepts.description: How wealth was transferred from India to Britain, the writers who documented it from Brooks Adams to Utsa Patnaik, and the symbolism of the 1778 painting 'The East offering its riches to Britannia'.
concepts.idea: Economic exploitation was not a side effect of British rule in India but the foundation of it.
concepts.rule: In 1895 the U.S. historian Brooks Adams wrote that the Bengal plunder began arriving in London soon after Plassey and that Britain's industrial revolution began with the year 1760; Will Durant called it the 'stolen wealth from India'. In 1901 Dadabhai Naoroji, the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, compiled from British reports the wealth drained out of India in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India', and Romesh Chunder Dutt did the same in his 'Economic History of India'; both showed many billions of pounds extracted. A recent estimate by Utsa Patnaik for 1765 to 1938 comes to 45 trillion U.S. dollars in today's value, about 13 times Britain's GDP in 2023. Wealth was taken not only through taxes but by charging Indians for the colonial power's own spending on the railways, the telegraph network and even on wars.

Dutt compile figures, Naoroji from Britain's own reports; Utsa Patnaik's recent estimate reaches 45 trillion US dollars for 1765 to 1938. concepts.name: Changing Landscapes: Industry, Governance, Education and the Colonial Economy
concepts.description: The four ways colonial rule reshaped Indian life: the ruin of indigenous industry, the dismantling of village self-governance and customary law, Macaulay's education policy, and an economy rebuilt to serve imperial needs.
concepts.idea: The colonial rulers were convinced India should be remade according to their own 'superior' conceptions, and they remade its industry, its government, its schools and its economy accordingly.
concepts.rule: Before the 18th century India was renowned for manufacturing, above all textiles in cotton, silk, wool, jute, hemp and coir. British policy imposed heavy duties on Indian textiles entering Britain while forcing India to accept British goods with minimal tariffs, and Britain controlled the sea trade and exchange rates, so Indian exports collapsed and skilled artisan communities were driven back onto overtaxed land; India's share of world GDP fell to hardly 5 per cent by Independence. Well-organised village councils that had managed community affairs, resolved disputes and built irrigation and roads were replaced by a centralised bureaucracy built for tax collection and order, and British codes of law disregarded customary practice, leaving courts that were expensive, slow and conducted in a foreign language. In education, Macaulay's 1835 Minute set out to create Indians 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect', and the traditional pathashalas, madrasas and viharas slowly disappeared. The economy itself was turned into a supplier of raw materials and a captive market, with railways laid out to carry raw materials to ports and troops to rebellions, and paid for by Indian taxes.
concepts.example: William Bentinck, then Governor-General, observed in 1834 that 'The bones of the cotton weavers are bleaching the plains of India.'

questions.a: Metcalfe was an acting Governor-General, so this is praise from inside the colonial administration rather than from a critic of it. He said the village communities had nearly everything they wanted within themselves, survived while dynasty after dynasty tumbled down, and had contributed more than any other cause to the preservation of the people of India. The awkwardness is that the British then systematically dismantled the very institution one of their own senior officials had called India's most durable, replacing it with a centralised bureaucracy built for tax collection and order rather than public welfare.

questions.q: The chapter says the British reshaped India's economy to serve imperial needs. Analyse what that economy was before, what it became, and give two pieces of evidence for the change.
questions.a: Before, India had a self-sufficient agricultural system supplemented by craft and manufacture production, renowned before the 18th century for its textiles and also producing iron, steel and paper. Afterwards it was a supplier of raw materials for British industry and a market forced to buy British manufactured goods. The first piece of evidence is trade policy: heavy duties on Indian textiles entering Britain, minimal tariffs on British goods entering India, and British control of the sea trade and exchange rates, so that Indian exports fell sharply while British imports rose faster still. The second is the railway network, laid out to move raw materials from the interior to the ports for export and to distribute British goods inland, largely ignoring existing trade patterns. The outcome was that India's share of world GDP fell to hardly 5 per cent by Independence, so that in less than two centuries one of the richest lands in the world had become one of the poorest.
s: Describes the economy before: self-sufficient agriculture with craft and manufacture
Describes what it became: raw-material supplier and captive market
First piece of evidence
Second piece of evidence

questions.q: Write a reply of about eight sentences to Macaulay's Minute, as a village schoolteacher in Bengal in 1835 might have written it.
questions.a: A sample reply: 'Sir, you write that a single shelf of a good European library is worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia, and in the same paper you admit that you read neither Sanskrit nor Arabic. I will not presume to weigh the books of your country, since I cannot read those either. Come instead and count what stands here. Your own government's reports say there are between one hundred thousand and one hundred and fifty thousand schools in Bengal and Bihar, and your own officers describe the system as economical, simple and effectual. In my school the children of this village learn reading, writing and arithmetic, and they learn them in their own language and beside their parents' work. You propose to replace this with an education designed to make them, in your words, English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect. Consider what that asks of a boy: to find his mother's speech beneath him and his grandfather ignorant. If what you want is clerks for your offices, say so plainly, but do not call it learning and do not tell us it is for our good.'

concepts.name: Early Resistance Movements before 1857
concepts.description: The four movements the chapter describes before the Great Rebellion: the Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion, the Kol Uprising, the Santhal Rebellion and the Indigo Revolt, and the British policies that provoked each.
concepts.idea: Almost from the beginning of British rule, people whose livelihoods had been taken away rose against it -- locally, repeatedly, and at great cost.
concepts.rule: The British called India 'the jewel in the crown of the British Empire' and asserted she would remain part of an empire 'on which the sun never sets'. Resistance began early. The Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion started in Bengal after the famine of 1770, when new land and taxation policies restricted the free movement of sannyasis (Hindu ascetics) and fakirs (Muslim ascetics); over three decades they attacked British treasuries and tax collectors, were called 'bandits', and were defeated by superior force. Tribal communities lost forest access and land, were taxed in cash, caught in debt traps, had their councils replaced and hundreds of their communities labelled 'criminal tribes'; the Kol Uprising of 1831-1832 in Chota Nagpur followed land policies favouring outsiders, and the Santhal Rebellion of 1855-1856 under Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu rose against moneylenders and landlords backed by the British. The Indigo Revolt of 1859-1862 answered European planters who forced Bengal peasants to grow indigo instead of food and trapped them in debt slavery.
concepts.example: The Sannyasi-Fakir rebellion later inspired Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel Anandamath of 1882, which contained the song 'Vande Mataram' -- India's national song after Independence.

questions.q: The four pre-1857 movements in this chapter involved very different people with different grievances. Analyse what they nonetheless had in common.
questions.a: All four were set off by British economic policy rather than by religion or dynastic ambition: new land and taxation policies restricted the sannyasis and fakirs, land policies favouring outsiders triggered the Kol Uprising, moneylenders and landlords taking ancestral lands with British support drove the Santhals, and forced indigo cultivation with debt slavery drove the Bengal peasants. In each case the people had first lost something they had held for generations -- free movement, forest and land rights, ancestral land, or the freedom to grow food. In each case the response was force: executions and superior forces against the sannyasis, the defeat of the Kols, burned villages and thousands of deaths among the Santhals, and mercenaries hired against the indigo peasants. And in each case the movement was local, which is why none of them threatened colonial rule as a whole in the way 1857 would.

concepts.name: The Great Rebellion of 1857 and the Legacy of Colonialism
concepts.description: The causes, course and suppression of the 1857 rebellion, the leaders who resisted, the Crown's takeover in 1858, and how the chapter weighs the legacy of colonial rule.
concepts.idea: The rebellion of 1857 failed militarily but sowed the idea that foreign domination was unacceptable, and colonial rule left a legacy the chapter insists on weighing honestly on both sides.
concepts.rule: The British called it the 'Sepoy Mutiny'; after Independence historians rejected that term and many, including this chapter, call it the Great Rebellion of 1857. Discontent was old -- the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 followed uniform regulations that violated Hindu and Muslim religious practice, and most sepoys came from agricultural families hurt by land revenue policy. In 1857 rumours that rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat offended both communities; Mangal Pandey attacked his officers at Barrackpore and was executed; sepoys at Meerut killed their officers, marched to Delhi and proclaimed the powerless Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. The revolt took Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi. The British response was systematic and extremely brutal, from house-to-house massacres in Delhi in September 1857 to mass executions at Kanpur and a long campaign of burned villages and destroyed crops. Some historians say the rebellion failed for want of a unified command and a consistent strategy. In 1858 the Crown took direct control from the Company, beginning the British Raj, and reorganised the Indian Army to prevent unified resistance.
concepts.example: The chapter holds two things together in its verdict: colonial rule was subjugation and exploitation, not a 'civilising mission' -- and it also, unintentionally, began the discipline of archaeology in India and carried Sanskrit texts to Europe, which Hegel likened to the discovery of a new continent.

At Kanpur they carried out mass executions designed to strike terror into the population. And in a long punitive campaign they burned villages and destroyed crops, causing countless deaths, vastly more than those inflicted by the rebels.

Most sepoys came from agricultural families that had been suffering great hardship because of British land revenue policies. And in 1857 itself, rumours that the rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat offended both communities.
s: The Vellore precedent and the uniform regulations

The greased cartridge rumours of 1857

questions.q: Trace the course of the Great Rebellion of 1857 in four stages, from the first incident to the change of government in 1858.
questions.a: First, at Barrackpore in present-day West Bengal the sepoy Mangal Pandey attacked British officers, and his execution spread further discontent while rumours about the greased cartridges circulated across northern and central India. Second, at Meerut in present-day Uttar Pradesh some sepoys killed their British officers and marched to nearby Delhi, where they proclaimed the elderly and politically powerless Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader, although the military decisions were actually taken by the commanders. Third, the revolt spread quickly across northern and central India, with sepoys capturing Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi; at Kanpur rebel forces under Nana Saheb first agreed to give safe passage to British civilians and then massacred over 200 men, women and children, for reasons still debated. Fourth, the British response was systematic and extremely brutal, beginning with the recapture of Delhi in September 1857, and in 1858 the British Crown took direct control of India from the East India Company and reorganised the Indian Army to prevent unified resistance in the future.
s: Stage one: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore and the cartridge rumours
Stage two: Meerut, the march to Delhi and Bahadur Shah Zafar
Stage three: the spread of the revolt and the events at Kanpur
Stage four: the British recapture and the Crown taking control in 1858

questions.q: In November 1858 Queen Victoria promised non-interference in religious matters and greater inclusion of Indians in the administration. Begum Hazrat Mahal answered with a counter-proclamation. Analyse why she did not trust the promise.
questions.a: She had direct experience of what British assurances were worth: her kingdom of Awadh had been annexed, and she had already refused an offer of safe passage in exchange for surrender. Her counter-proclamation warned Indians that it is the unvarying custom of the English never to forgive a fault, be it great or small, meaning that promises made at the moment of victory would not protect anyone who had resisted. Since the proclamation came in the same year as the mass executions and the punitive burning of villages, she had very recent evidence on her side.
s: Refers to the annexation of Awadh or her refusal of safe passage
States the substance of her counter-proclamation
Connects her distrust to the British conduct of the suppression

questions.q: The chapter denies that colonial rule was a 'civilising mission' yet still lists real gains. Analyse its position, naming two gains and the cost attached to each.
questions.a: The chapter's position is that the gains were largely unintended consequences of a process whose purpose was subjugation and exploitation, executed systematically and with brutal repression, so they do not redeem it; and it removes the ground for a civilising mission by noting that India's own civilisation was much older than Europe's. The first gain is documentation: the British surveyed the Subcontinent meticulously, listed its ethnic groups, studied India's monuments and their art and architecture, restored some ruined ones and initiated the discipline of archaeology. The cost attached is that the ethnic lists were flawed by the unscientific notion of 'race', which genetics has since shown does not exist, and that thousands of statues, paintings, jewels, manuscripts and other artefacts were stolen and sent to European museums and private collections. The second gain is the flow of Sanskrit texts to Europe, which Georg Hegel likened to the discovery of a new continent and which influenced European philosophers, writers, poets and artists. Its cost is subtler: some of the scholars behind it were not admirers of Indian culture at all, but believed that studying Indian languages and texts would make it easier to demonstrate the superiority of Christianity.
s: States the chapter's overall position on the 'civilising mission'
First gain, correctly described
Second gain, correctly described
Attaches a genuine cost to each gain rather than a general complaint

questions.q: Some argue that looted Indian artefacts have been better preserved abroad than they would have been in India. Weigh this argument using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter allows that the removal promoted some appreciation of Indian art among the European public, so the argument is not empty. But it calls the theft a profound cultural loss and a violation of India's heritage, and preservation elsewhere does not settle the question of ownership: an object kept safely is still an object taken. The chapter also records that the British restored ruined monuments in India and began the discipline of archaeology there, which weakens any claim that India could not have looked after its own. It leaves the repatriation debate deliberately open, and on this evidence the preservation argument is a reason for care in returning objects, not a reason to keep them.
s: Concedes the strongest point on the other side
Gives the chapter's counter-evidence on cultural loss or ownership
Reaches a judgement rather than simply restating both sides

questions.q: Write a front-page news report of about eight sentences, as a Delhi newspaper might have published it in 1858, on the year that has just ended.
questions.a: A sample report: 'The rule of the East India Company in India has ended. From this year authority passes directly to the British Crown, and a proclamation issued in November in the name of Queen Victoria promises non-interference in religious matters and a greater place for Indians in the administration. The change follows a year of rebellion that began with sepoys at Meerut, who killed their officers and rode to this city, where the aged emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was proclaimed their leader although the fighting was directed by the commanders. The revolt reached Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi, and in each place it has now been put down. The recapture of this city in September was accompanied by killing from house to house, and in the countryside villages have been burned and crops destroyed in a campaign that continues. The rebel leaders are scattered: the Rani of Jhansi fell in battle in June, and Begum Hazrat Mahal has crossed into Nepal, issuing a proclamation of her own that warns readers the English never forgive a fault, be it great or small. Observers say the rising failed for want of a single command and a settled plan. Whether the promises made in the Queen's name will be kept is a question this paper cannot answer, and many of its readers have already formed a view.'
s: Written as a news report of 1858 rather than as an essay
Reports the transfer of power to the Crown and Victoria's proclamation
Summarises the course of the rebellion accurately
Includes at least two named individuals, correctly
Keeps a reporting voice and runs to roughly the length asked for
